title: Berkshire Hathaway Repurchases $9.6 Billion of Stock Amid Falling Profits【AP】
body:
Berkshire Hathaway disclosed that it bought back $9.6 billion of its own shares during the third quarter, even as the conglomerate’s quarterly earnings fell sharply. The repurchase, which lifted the total buyback tally for the year to roughly $28 billion, came against a backdrop of a 28 percent drop in net profit, driven largely by weaker performance at its flagship insurance arm, GEICO, and a decline in the market value of its investment portfolio.

The Omaha‑based holding company reported earnings of $7.2 billion for the three months ended September 30, compared with $10 billion a year earlier. While operating earnings from its core businesses – insurance, railroads, utilities and manufacturing – remained solid, the loss of value in publicly traded holdings such as Apple, Bank of America and a suite of energy stocks pulled the consolidated bottom line down. Analysts note that the decline is less a sign of operational weakness and more a reflection of volatile equity markets that have eroded the fair‑value adjustments required under U.S. GAAP.

GEICO, Berkshire’s largest insurance subsidiary, was a particular drag on results. Premium growth slowed to 1.5 percent year‑over‑year, and the carrier’s combined ratio – a key profitability metric – widened to 99.7 percent from 97.2 percent the previous year. The insurer attributed the shift to higher advertising spend, as it sought to capture market share in a highly competitive auto‑insurance landscape, and to an uptick in claims severity linked to rising vehicle repair costs. Although the company’s loss‑ratio remained stable, the higher expense ratio squeezed underwriting profit, prompting a downgrade of its earnings outlook by several brokerage houses.

Despite the earnings dip, Berkshire’s board continued to endorse an aggressive share‑repurchase strategy. The company’s chief financial officer, Ajit Jain, explained that the buyback program is intended to return excess capital to shareholders while the market undervalues Berkshire’s long‑term earnings power. “We have a sizable cash pile, and repurchasing shares at these levels is a disciplined way to enhance per‑share metrics,” he said in a conference call. The repurchase also serves to offset dilution from stock‑based compensation and to signal confidence in the firm’s future cash‑flow generation.

Investors have reacted with mixed sentiment. The stock rose modestly in after‑hours trading following the announcement, but some value‑focused funds expressed concern that the buyback could be “premature” given the recent earnings weakness. Critics argue that allocating capital to share repurchases rather than bolstering underwriting reserves or pursuing strategic acquisitions may limit Berkshire’s ability to capitalize on emerging opportunities, especially in the rapidly evolving insurance technology space.

Looking ahead, Berkshire’s performance will hinge on several variables. First, the trajectory of the broader equity market will affect the unrealized gains or losses on its investment holdings, which currently account for a sizable share of its net worth. Second, GEICO’s ability to translate higher advertising spend into sustainable premium growth without eroding profitability will be closely watched. Finally, the conglomerate’s capital‑allocation committee is expected to evaluate whether to continue the current pace of buybacks or to pivot toward new acquisitions, particularly in sectors such as renewable energy and fintech where Buffett’s protégé, Greg Abel, has signaled interest. As the fourth quarter approaches, market participants will gauge whether Berkshire can rebound from the profit slump while maintaining its disciplined return‑of‑capital strategy.
